pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Skeletons & Muscles

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Animals, including humans'):** "identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE):** NGSS has no dedicated skeleton/muscle performance expectation at this grade band; the nearest structural-function ideas sit in 4-LS1-1 (internal/external structures that support survival) and MS-LS1-3 (body as interacting subsystems). Treat this as a UK-led topic and flag the divergence.

- **Operational details:** Children learn the three jobs of the skeleton — support (holds the body up, gives shape), protection (skull guards the brain; ribcage guards heart and lungs), and movement (bones are levers that muscles pull on). Introduce that muscles work by CONTRACTING (getting shorter and pulling) and cannot push, which is why they work in antagonistic pairs (biceps/triceps at the elbow). Compare a vertebrate skeleton (internal, bony endoskeleton) with animals that have exoskeletons (insects) or no skeleton (worms, jellyfish — hydrostatic). Anchor everything in the child's own body: feel your own ribs, skull, backbone; feel a muscle bulge and shorten when you bend your elbow.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A Y3 child can name the three functions, point to protective bones on their own body, and feel a muscle contract — but the antagonistic-pair mechanism (one pulls while its partner relaxes) is the transitional step where misconceptions cluster.
bestPractices: Ground it in the child's own body first: have them feel their skull, ribs, backbone and knee/elbow joints before looking at any diagram, so the skeleton is felt as real structure, not a Halloween picture.
Teach the three functions (support, protection, movement) as the organising spine of the topic and keep returning to them — every bone example should be tagged to at least one function.

Make the muscle mechanism kinaesthetic: bend the elbow and feel the biceps shorten and harden; this establishes that muscles PULL by contracting and never push, the key idea for the antagonistic pair.
Use a real physical lever or a card-and-split-pin model of the elbow so the child sees bone-as-lever and muscle-as-string, connecting to their forces learning.
Contrast body plans (human endoskeleton vs insect exoskeleton vs boneless worm/jellyfish) so 'skeleton' is understood as one solution among several, not a universal given.
Name protective bones precisely (cranium/skull → brain; ribcage → heart and lungs; spine → spinal cord) so protection is concrete, not a slogan.
keyRepresentations: A labelled whole-body skeleton diagram with major bones (skull, ribcage, spine, femur) colour-coded by function
The elbow-joint model: two 'bones' hinged, with a biceps and triceps drawn as bands that shorten/lengthen — the canonical antagonistic-pair representation
A hinge-joint card-and-split-pin manipulative (bone levers + elastic muscle) the child can move
Comparison strip: human (endoskeleton) / beetle (exoskeleton) / earthworm (no skeleton) side by side
'Feel-your-own-body' body map marking where you can feel skull, ribs, spine, and a working muscle
commonMisconceptions: Thinking muscles can push — children assume a muscle straightens the arm by pushing; in fact each muscle only pulls (contracts), so a second muscle is needed to move the bone back.
Believing bones are dead, dry, or non-living like the plastic ones in a display — living bone is active tissue with blood supply that grows and repairs.
Assuming only the arms and legs 'have' a skeleton, missing that the skull, ribs and spine are skeleton too.
Confusing 'skeleton' with 'the hard bits' generally and lumping in teeth or nails, or thinking all animals have bones inside (so an insect's hard shell is 'its bones').
Thinking a single muscle both bends AND straightens a joint, rather than an antagonistic pair taking turns.

learn.summary: Skeletons and muscles for 7–8 year-olds: the three jobs of the skeleton (support, protection, movement), that bones are living tissue, and that muscles move bones by CONTRACTING (shortening and pulling) and never by pushing — which is why they work in antagonistic pairs such as the biceps and triceps at the elbow. Learning is anchored in the child's own body (feeling ribs, skull, spine and a muscle bulging) and extended to compare body plans (human endoskeleton, insect exoskeleton, boneless worm/jellyfish).

activities.title: Elbow rig: discover that muscles pull, never push
feedback: If the learner expects the biceps to also lower the arm: a muscle can only shorten and pull, so pulling the biceps can never push the forearm back down — watch what happens when the triceps underneath contracts instead.
If the learner succeeds in lowering the arm with the triceps: notice the biceps had to relax (lengthen) while the triceps pulled — the pair takes turns.
Reinforce: when you felt your real biceps harden, that hardening IS the muscle contracting and pulling the bone.
activities.rationale: A manipulable hinged arm with contracting/relaxing bands lets the learner test the 'muscles push' prediction and see it fail, making the antagonistic-pair mechanism observable rather than asserted. The draggable bands, rotating bone lever and the deliberately-failing 'lower it with the biceps only' challenge are optional interaction examples that make the pull-only mechanism concrete; a card-and-split-pin arm model with an elastic 'muscle' achieves the same idea with physical materials. Pairing with the child's own felt arm keeps it grounded in real anatomy.
sourceClaims: Muscles work by contracting (pulling) and act in antagonistic pairs such as the biceps and triceps at the elbow; a muscle cannot push a bone back, so its partner must contract — a common area of pupil misconception.
DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement'.
learnerActions: Look at an arm shown as two hinged 'bones' meeting at the elbow, with a biceps band above and a triceps band below.
Activate (drag/tap) the biceps so it shortens and thickens, and watch the forearm swing UP — note that the muscle got shorter and the bone moved.

Take the challenge: 'Now put the arm back down using ONLY the biceps.' Try, and notice that in the rig (which has no gravity pulling on it) contracting the biceps only pulls the forearm up, so it can never push the arm back down.
Activate the triceps and watch the forearm swing back down; state in your own words why a second muscle was needed.

Feel your own biceps harden as you bend your real elbow (try lifting a light book), then feel it go soft when you let your arm rest straight on a table — connect the rig to what your arm is already doing.
activities.intendedInsight: A muscle moves a bone only by getting shorter and pulling; it cannot push. Because of this, a second muscle (its antagonistic partner) is needed to actively pull the bone back the other way — one muscle alone cannot both bend and straighten a joint (gravity can let an arm drop, but no muscle can push it).

activities.title: Feel-your-own-body skeleton map and protective bones
feedback: If the learner names only support: the skeleton also protects (skull guards the brain, ribs guard the heart and lungs) and enables movement when muscles pull on bones.
If the learner thinks only arms and legs have a skeleton: the skull, ribcage and spine are skeleton too — feel your own ribs and backbone.
If the learner says bones are dead like a display skeleton: living bone has a blood supply and grows and repairs.
If the learner thinks an insect's shell is 'its bones inside': that hard outer case is an exoskeleton, a different body plan.
activities.rationale: Grounding naming and protection in the child's own felt body first makes the skeleton real rather than a Halloween picture, and keeps the three functions as the organising spine of the topic. Colour-coding bones by function and viewing how the ribcage encloses the heart and lungs make the protection idea concrete. Tap-to-reveal bone facts and lift-the-flap myth-busters are optional interaction examples that surface the 'bones are dead' and 'insects have bones inside' misconceptions; the same can be done with a physical labelled diagram and discussion.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement'.
learnerActions: Before looking at any diagram, feel your own skull, ribs, backbone and the hinge at your elbow and knee.
On a labelled whole-body skeleton with major bones (skull, ribcage, spine, femur) colour-coded by function, locate each bone you just felt on your own body.
Match protective bones to what they guard: cranium/skull → brain; ribcage → heart and lungs; spine → spinal cord.

Look at how the ribcage wraps around and encloses the heart and lungs — ideally viewing it from more than one side — and tag each bone example to at least one of the three jobs: support, protection, movement.
Open 'myth-buster' flaps and decide: are bones dead and dry, or living tissue? Does an insect have bones inside its hard shell?
activities.intendedInsight: The skeleton does three jobs — support, protection and movement — and includes the skull, ribs and spine, not just arms and legs. Named bones protect specific organs (the ribcage curving around the heart and lungs), and living bone is active tissue, not the dry plastic of a display.

activities.title: Compare body plans: endoskeleton, exoskeleton, no hard skeleton
feedback: If the learner says all animals have bones inside: a beetle's support is a hard outer case (exoskeleton), and worms and jellyfish have no bones at all.
If the learner is unsure why a jellyfish can't stand: it has no rigid internal skeleton to hold its shape up against gravity.
activities.rationale: Contrasting body plans prevents the overgeneralisation that every animal has an internal bony skeleton and clarifies the exoskeleton confusion, supporting the 'some other animals' part of the standard.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory requirement: 'identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement'.
learnerActions: Look side by side at a human (bony skeleton inside), a beetle (hard case outside), and an earthworm or jellyfish (no bones).
Describe where the hard supporting structure is for each: inside the body, outside the body, or with no hard parts at all (soft bodies held in shape by fluid or water).
Answer: why can't a jellyfish stand up the way you can — what does your body have that it doesn't?
Explain why an insect's hard shell is NOT the same as having bones inside.
activities.intendedInsight: A bony internal skeleton is one solution among several for support and protection — some animals have a hard external skeleton and some, like worms and jellyfish, have no bones or hard skeleton at all — so 'having a bony skeleton' is not universal and 'hard bits outside' are not bones inside.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: which muscle straightens the arm?
feedback: If the learner predicts the top muscle pushes the arm straight: feel the triceps at the back of the upper arm tighten as you straighten against resistance — that muscle pulls the bone while the biceps relaxes.
On the matching task: check that skull→brain and ribcage→heart and lungs are paired correctly.
Watch for the idea that 'muscles push the bone' — use it as a cue to re-feel the arm and re-run the elbow rig.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain cycle on the learner's own arm directly targets the dominant 'muscles push' misconception by letting the felt evidence contradict the prediction. Categorisation and matching consolidate the three functions and protective-bone pairings; note that recognition-style sorting/matching checks and reinforces knowledge but does not by itself elicit the learner constructing the pull-mechanism explanation, which the rig and POE steps provide.
sourceClaims: Muscles work by contracting (pulling) and act in antagonistic pairs such as the biceps and triceps at the elbow; a muscle cannot push a bone back, so its partner must contract — a common area of pupil misconception.
learnerActions: Bend your arm and feel the biceps on top harden; then straighten it.
PREDICT which muscle tightens to straighten the arm, and say why.
Straighten the arm against a little resistance (e.g. press your hand down on a table or against a partner's hand) and feel the back of your upper arm — notice the triceps tightening.
Explain what has to happen to move the bone back, given that a muscle can only pull.
Sort a set of bones by their job (support / protect / move), and match each protective bone to the organ it guards.
activities.intendedInsight: When you actively straighten your arm (for example, against resistance) the triceps at the back of the upper arm pulls, not the biceps pushing — muscles pull in opposition, and naming/sorting bones by function consolidates the three jobs.

constraints: UK-led topic: NGSS has no dedicated skeleton/muscle performance expectation at this grade band; the nearest structure–function ideas sit in 4-LS1-1 (internal/external structures supporting survival) and MS-LS1-3 (body as interacting subsystems). Flag this divergence for US contexts.

Checkpoint is concrete/observational (Tier A): a 7–8 year-old can name the three functions, point to protective bones on their own body, and feel a muscle contract. The antagonistic-pair mechanism (one pulls while its partner relaxes) is the transitional step where misconceptions cluster and needs the most support.

Sorting, matching and multiple-choice tasks reinforce and check naming and function but do not on their own require the learner to independently construct the pull-only mechanism explanation; include the elbow rig and felt-arm POE for that.
Card-and-split-pin or screen-based elbow models are approximations of real bones, joints and muscles; always connect them back to the child feeling their own arm so the model explains real anatomy.
Keep the three functions (support, protection, movement) as the organising spine and tag every bone example to at least one function; name protective bones precisely rather than as slogans.

An in-role 'ask the skeleton' chat can provide light framing or prompt a child to explain their thinking, but it does not itself supply the physical manipulation or felt-body experience this mechanical content calls for; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on work.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources (BBC Bitesize; NGSS 4-LS1-1) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat claim strength accordingly.

The legacy entry asserted a 2D rig 'directly kills' the misconception and that a static image 'cannot make the muscle-contraction mechanism felt'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened: a manipulable model makes the mechanism observable and is well suited here, but a static diagram plus felt-arm work can still teach it. The dialogue format was rated 'poor' in the legacy row; this has been retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance/limitation, not a universal law.

The legacy 3D-interactive entry was downgraded as 'nice-to-have'; its genuine affordance (seeing how the ribcage encloses heart/lungs in the round, from more than one side) is now explicitly carried inside the protection activity rather than kept as a separate ranked option.

The DfE claim is attached to multiple activities as the curricular basis; it directly supports the naming/protection and 'some other animals' principles, and is retained on the mechanism activity only as curriculum grounding for the movement function, with the BBC claim carrying the pull-mechanism principle.
The original row notes worms/jellyfish are 'hydrostatic'; this nuance is simplified to 'no bones / no rigid internal skeleton' for this age band — accurate but not the full picture.

assess.poeTask: Have each child bend their arm and feel the biceps on top harden, then straighten it. Ask them to PREDICT which muscle tightens to straighten the arm and why. Many predict the top muscle 'pushes' it straight; feeling the triceps underneath tighten instead shows muscles pull and work in opposition.
probeDeeper: When you straighten your bent arm, which muscle do you think pulls — the one on top or the one underneath?
Which bones protect your brain, and which protect your heart and lungs?
If a muscle can only pull and never push, what has to happen to move the bone back again?
Why can't a jellyfish stand up the way you can — what does your body have that it doesn't?
assess.correctAnswer: A muscle moves a bone by pulling: as it gets shorter it pulls the bone. It cannot push. So one muscle can pull the bone one way, but a different muscle is needed to pull it back — one muscle alone cannot both bend and straighten the arm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Muscles push bones to move them ('the muscle pushes my arm straight')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Muscles can only shorten and pull; that's exactly why a second muscle is needed to move the bone back. Feel the arm's muscles while bending and straightening.
errorPatterns.distractor: The muscle pushes the bone to straighten the arm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a muscle straightens the arm by pushing the bone

errorPatterns.pattern: The skeleton's only job is to hold you upright
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw out all three jobs: support, protect (skull→brain, ribs→heart and lungs) and enable movement with muscles.
errorPatterns.distractor: The skeleton's only job is to keep you standing up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names support but not protection or movement when asked what the skeleton does

errorPatterns.pattern: Muscles work on their own, not attached to bones
errorPatterns.nextMove: Muscles are anchored to bones; when they pull, the bone moves. Use a simple hinged-arm model with an elastic 'muscle'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about muscles moving but never connects them to pulling on bones

responseLevels.gap: Thinks muscles push, or names only one function of the skeleton; doesn't connect muscle to bone.
responseLevels.full: Explains muscles pull bones (never push) so movement needs muscles working against each other, and gives all three skeletal functions with protection examples.
responseLevels.partial: Knows muscles move bones and can name protection examples, but still says a muscle pushes, or misses that a second muscle is needed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A muscle is joined to a bone, and when it works it gets shorter and tighter. So how does a muscle actually make a bone move — by pushing the bone away, or by pulling it? And can one single muscle both bend your arm and straighten it again on its own?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands muscle action says muscles pull (never push) and therefore need a partner. A child without it says a muscle pushes the bone straight, treating the muscle like a rigid rod, and sees no need for a second muscle.
